title: 3-Read Friday #54: Assessment Design, Lesson Objectives, and AI in Teaching
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 54 gathers three picks on assessment theory, lesson design, and AI's likely impact on teaching. Barton opens with Daisy Christodoulou's first instalment on designing an assessment system, praising her as the best writer on assessment and summarising her framing of the tension between assessing understanding and holding schools accountable. He then recommends Dylan Kane's argument that lesson objectives are 'overrated', posing a string of rhetorical questions about where retrieval practice, prerequisite checks, and other unstated goals fit into a single tidy objective. His third pick is Larry Cuban's reflective post on whether AI will transform teaching, which Barton frames through his own oscillating feelings of intrigue, excitement, and concern about AI's classroom impact.
points: Barton's framing of Christodoulou as writing better on assessment than almost anyone signals just how central her No More Marking series is to his own thinking about accountability versus formative purpose.

His summary of Kane's piece highlights the specific unstated goals (retrieval practice, prerequisite checks, method selection, feelings of success) that a single lesson objective can't capture -- showing he engaged with the argument's specifics, not just its headline.
Barton's admission that he 'flicks between' intrigue, excitement, and concern about AI several times a day models an unresolved, honest stance rather than either AI-hype or AI-dismissal.

Pairing an assessment-theory piece with a lesson-design critique and an AI reflection in one issue shows Barton deliberately curating across different layers of the profession (system, classroom, and technology) rather than three variations on one theme.
quotes: Here are three blog posts that I found interesting this week.

Nobody writes better about assessment than Daisy. In the first post in this series, Daisy looks at two conflicting purposes of assessment: to assess students’ understanding and to hold teachers and schools to account.
Lesson objectives force teachers to ensure each phase of their lesson is in service of those objectives.
Where does retrieval practice fit in? How about prerequisite knowledge checks, method selection, creating feelings of success, and all the other “objectives” that do not fit into tidy sentences?

If, like me, you are intrigued / excited / concerned (I flick between these states several times a day) by the impact AI could have on teaching and learning, you should find this reflection by Larry interesting.
